Each image was a window to a life that felt increasingly distant, yet the memories they evoked were suffocating. One particular photo reminded her of a day that had changed everything. It was a sunny afternoon four years ago when a terrorist attack occurred during a public event she was attending. Rina had been in the thick of it, witnessing chaos and fear that left an indelible mark on her psyche. Now, even the faintest scent of alcohol could send her spiraling back to that moment, as it reminded her of a friend who had been drinking nearby, their laughter cut short by the sudden violence. In the months following the attack, Rina found herself grappling with overwhelming feelings that she could neither name nor contain. To cope, she developed maladaptive strategies that offered temporary relief but left her feeling worse in the long run. She threw herself into excessive exercise, believing that if she could push her body to its limits, perhaps she could outrun the emotional pain that gripped her. But this compulsive behavior was a double-edged sword; it only deepened her sense of inadequacy when she inevitably faced moments of weakness. Each time she turned to exercise or food as a coping mechanism, she reinforced her belief that the world was a threatening place, as if her inability to manage her emotions validated her fears of being overwhelmed by life. On other days, when the weight of her feelings became too much, she would turn to food, overeating to distract herself from the chaos in her mind. At her lowest moments, she resorted to self-harm - a desperate attempt to release the pent-up anguish she could not articulate. Each act of harm felt like a temporary reprieve, yet it only reinforced her belief that she was out of control, further entrenching her negative appraisals of herself and the world. Rina, a 57-year-old interior designer of South Eastern Asian descent, sat in her softly lit living room, looking through old photographs. Each image was a window to a life that felt increasingly distant, yet the memories they evoked were suffocating. One particular photo reminded her of a day that had changed everything. It was a sunny afternoon four years ago when a terrorist attack occurred during a public event she was attending. Rina had been in the thick of it, witnessing chaos and fear that left an indelible mark on her psyche. Now, even the faintest scent of alcohol could send her spiraling back to that moment, as it reminded her of a friend who had been drinking nearby, their laughter cut short by the sudden violence. 

In the months following the attack, Rina found herself grappling with overwhelming feelings that she could neither name nor contain. To cope, she developed maladaptive strategies that offered temporary relief but left her feeling worse in the long run. She threw herself into excessive exercise, believing that if she could push her body to its limits, perhaps she could outrun the emotional pain that gripped her. But this compulsive behavior was a double-edged sword; it only deepened her sense of inadequacy when she inevitably faced moments of weakness. Each time she turned to exercise or food as a coping mechanism, she reinforced her belief that the world was a threatening place, as if her inability to manage her emotions validated her fears of being overwhelmed by life. On other days, when the weight of her feelings became too much, she would turn to food, overeating to distract herself from the chaos in her mind. At her lowest moments, she resorted to self-harm — a desperate attempt to release the pent-up anguish she could not articulate. Each act of harm felt like a temporary reprieve, yet it only reinforced her belief that she was out of control, further entrenching her negative appraisals of herself and the world. Rina had come to see her self-harm as a necessary outlet for the chaos within, wrongly believing that by inflicting pain, she could regain a sense of control and distance herself from her overwhelming emotional state. However, each act of self-harm only deepened her sense of threat, as it confirmed her belief that she was unable to cope with her emotions in healthier ways, leaving her feeling more vulnerable than ever.

Rina's hypervigilance became a constant companion. She felt that she had to be on guard all the time, ever watchful for threats that might emerge from the shadows. This incessant alertness was exhausting but seemed necessary; she had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place, one where harm could strike at any moment. Her conviction that she was permanently vulnerable made every unfamiliar situation feel like a potential threat, as she anticipated danger lurking behind every corner and in every interaction. In response to this perceived threat, she found herself planning her exits from every room, convinced that staying alert was the only way to protect herself from potential danger. She often found herself scanning the faces of strangers, looking for signs of potential danger, a habit that made her feel both empowered and trapped. This hyperawareness was a direct response to her traumatic experience, as thoughts of the attack replayed in her mind, leading to flashbacks that felt hauntingly real. Each flashback served as a reminder that the threat was ongoing, solidifying her belief that she could never truly relax or feel safe, further fueling her urge to engage in safety behaviors. Having internalized the belief that she was inherently vulnerable, Rina found herself anticipating danger at every turn, convinced that any unfamiliar situation could erupt into chaos without warning. Whenever someone touched her unexpectedly, she would startle, her heart racing as if she were back in that chaotic moment, the sounds of panic echoing in her ears. 

These negative appraisals colored her perception of everyday interactions. Rina felt increasingly isolated as she withdrew from social gatherings. Each time she felt the anxiety rise at the thought of being around others, she would tell herself that avoiding the event was the only way to protect herself from being overwhelmed again, reinforcing her reliance on these maladaptive strategies. The thought of attending an event would trigger a wave of anxiety, prompting her to leave early or avoid them altogether; she convinced herself that staying too long would only increase her chances of being overwhelmed again. The mere thought of attending an event would trigger a wave of anxiety, prompting her to leave early or avoid them altogether; she convinced herself that staying too long would only increase her chances of being overwhelmed again. Conversations about the event were particularly triggering; even discussing it with close friends felt like opening a wound that had never healed. The more she avoided these topics, the more she became entrenched in her own fears, convinced that her emotional fragility was a burden to others. These negative appraisals of her emotional state would trigger intense anxiety whenever she encountered reminders of the attack, pushing her to withdraw even further from conversations that might open old wounds. She often found herself trapped in a cycle, where the avoidance of certain places or conversations only deepened her sense of danger and unpredictability in the world. 

Rina recognized that her maladaptive strategies were not just temporary fixes; they were symptomatic of a deeper struggle with her mental health. This realization came when she sat down with her husband, who expressed concern about her well-being. She could no longer deny how her coping mechanisms, rather than alleviating her distress, were reinforcing her fears and negative beliefs. The truth was, she felt both helpless and ashamed. It was a paradox, but she understood that her strategies were not only a way to cope but also a form of self-punishment, reinforcing her belief that she could not deal with even the slightest upset.

Eventually, the cumulative effect of her symptoms brought Rina to a breaking point. She felt trapped in her own life, longing for the peace she had lost but unsure how to reclaim it. It was the overwhelming weight of her suffering that finally compelled her to seek help, though she was terrified of what that might mean. Rina hoped to find a path towards healing, but what frightened her most was the fear that she might never escape the shadows of her past.
